Free Trade. The economic principle that goods and services should move across borders without tariffs, quotas, or other protective barriers, determined by market forces rather than government intervention. This doctrine, also known as laissez-faire when applied to all economic sectors, was championed by Adam Smith and later codified as economic policy during the Industrial Revolution.

Adam Smith's Wealth of Nations, published in 1776, laid the philosophical groundwork for free trade by arguing that self-interest and competition drive efficient production and lower prices. The doctrine asserts comparative advantage, meaning nations should specialize in goods they produce most efficiently and trade for others, benefiting the entire world economy. The Industrial Revolution accelerated free trade adoption as British manufacturers, confident in their technological superiority, sought unrestricted export markets. Britain's commitment to free trade reached its peak when the corn laws, which had imposed tariffs protecting English grain producers, were repealed in 1846 after decades of campaigning by the Anti Corn Law League. This marked free trade's political triumph in Britain and became the dominant ideology of nineteenth-century Britain. Yet protectionism, the opposite philosophy, resurged during economic crises, notably the Great Depression, with nations raising tariffs in response to competitive devaluation. Modern free trade is embodied in institutions like the World Trade Organization and trade agreements like NAFTA, though these agreements typically contain many exceptions and carve-outs for political interests.
